skills.name: Guided preparation: a business plan for a locality

note.text: This classroom project prepares a reasoned plan rather than registering or launching a real business. Identify a possible local need, the intended customers, resources, proposed ownership and likely costs. A need is not automatically paying demand: customers must be willing and able to buy at a viable price. Separate initial equipment from funds needed for everyday operations. A plan should identify what is known, assumed and still to be checked. Learners do not have to spend money or disclose household finances.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text: By the end, you should be able to justify a fictional business choice using demand, resources, ownership and a simple budget. Builds on: ownership comparisons, financing and enterprise objectives. Leads to: scale, growth and location decisions that test the plan further.

sections.heading: Understand the economics

sections.heading: Follow the local case
sections.text: An imaginary Buea repair service proposes a small work space, tools and funds for materials. The group explains why its service might be useful, how ownership would work and what evidence would test demand. It lists appropriate permissions as matters to verify, without inventing a current filing checklist or suggesting that classroom approval is legal authorisation.

sections.heading: Reason and check
sections.text: Write a short exercise-book plan: proposed service; customers and evidence needed; resources; ownership choice with a limitation; labelled budget; risks and checks. Use fictional figures. Review whether funds cover both setup and initial operations, then explain one uncertainty the arithmetic cannot settle.

cards.idea: Distinguish these features before judging a business.
example: demand evidence: information about willingness and ability to buy the proposed service.
fixed equipment: durable resources used repeatedly in the activity.
working funds: resources available to support everyday operations.
feasibility check: testing whether a proposal fits its constraints and evidence.

cards.idea: Use the stated case evidence to identify the economic feature.
example: The group asks what would show that customers could actually pay.
The plan identifies tools used across many repairs.
The plan allows funds for materials and routine outgoings.
The group checks funds, skills, demand and matters needing authorisation.

cards.idea: Explain a consequence instead of assuming every option has the same effect.
example: demand evidence: Demand needs evidence about potential customers, not just the proposer’s enthusiasm.
fixed equipment: Equipment and recurring operating payments are different categories.
working funds: A business can have tools yet lack funds to meet current expenses.
feasibility check: A budget checks one constraint; demand, capability and other conditions still matter.

questions.prompt: A fictional classroom plan has {funds} CFA francs of confirmed funds. Planned equipment costs {equipment} and initial working funds {working}. How much remains after both allocations?

misconceptions.explain: You omitted the initial working-fund allocation.
Costs and allocations reduce the remaining budget, not increase it.
